findings.detail: Phase 3.3 could have been satisfied by a sentence saying two bugs were fixed. It was not. Spec lines 99-102 now state the rule, not the patch: a slot owner's process start is an ISO-8601 UTC identity, liveness requires both PID and parsed UTC start to survive JSON DateTime/DateTimeOffset/string round-trips, and a malformed or reused identity is a dead owner rather than a match. Lines 144-148 do the same for the stdout lock: child stdout is diagnostic only, durable fallback may accept completion only from a watcher terminal event, and nonterminal or send-uncertain state can neither become completed nor release capacity without separate proof. Lines 164-168 then turn both into required unit coverage, including the negative case. That is the difference between recording a repair and recording a contract, and it is what survives when this task folder is archived.

The rate-limiting case, which never happened during the test, is now written down plainly as proven only by unit tests rather than being quietly counted as passed. And the two browser script files themselves remain outside what I am allowed to read, so for those three fixes I am relying on the independent review and the new tests rather than my own reading. pmReview.productManagerStatement: I recommend accepting this milestone. This was the foundation step, and it did what it promised. Before this change, everything in your GPT Pro bridge shared one single lock, so two Chrome tabs could never work at the same time, the send record did not remember which Codex task it belonged to, and the caller had no way to say exactly which tab to use. All three of those are now addressed. The rules are also written into the permanent tooling document rather than only into this task's folder, which matters because I can read that document myself: it now says that every send, wait, response and run must carry one exact task identity, that a page is claimed atomically before anything is typed or clicked, that a claim never expires on a timer and never lets a crash be treated as permission to send again, that the lock is now derived from the full identity of a specific tab so an unknown or half-specified target is refused rather than allowed to slip through as its own separate lock, and that a long wait no longer keeps holding the lock while it sits there polling. Your existing guarantees were re-tested and pass: 159 adapter tests, 67 watcher tests, the project consistency checks all clean with nothing blocking. A dedicated check confirmed three genuinely different tabs get three separate locks and all three can proceed. I want to be straight with you about three things, none of which is a reason to hold this up. First, one item on the checklist is ticked but only half done: the team was supposed to write the two-hour default wait and the two special result names for a stuck or never-started page into that permanent tooling document, and those four things are not there. They are correctly written in the requirements and design, so nothing is at risk today, but they should be added before the next milestone starts so the next stage cannot quietly use different names or a different default. Second, two of the five small suggestions from your last approval were not picked up: booking your Chrome session at the start of the next milestone rather than at its end, and adding a step to actually look at the waiting-time measurements before deciding whether anything needs to be fairer between two competing tasks. Both are one-line edits. Third, one of the two outside reviewers, Grok, could not run at all because of a setup fault in its own reviewing profile, so only Antigravity actually reviewed the code, and it found nothing blocking. The same fault will happen again next time unless it is fixed. One coverage caveat that is not the team's fault and has not changed: the review snapshot deliberately excludes the installed Skill and plugin files, so I still cannot open the actual PowerShell adapter. What I can do is compare fingerprints, and that comparison is reassuring: the adapter and watcher fingerprints both changed from the values recorded at planning time, the shared bridge file's fingerprint did not change at all, and that is exactly the pattern this milestone was supposed to produce. Finally, be clear about what you are accepting. This is roughly a third of the engineering work, and none of the eleven things you actually care about are proven yet. Nothing has run against real ChatGPT pages, no batch of three requests has run, and the known unsafe file-writing in the bridge is still there because it is deliberately scheduled for the next milestone. What you have is the safety machinery that makes the next milestone possible without risking a double send.

findings.detail: At M1 I recorded a medium data-integrity risk: the bridge still picked session directories with a non-atomic exists loop and rewrote the shared task evidence file with an unlocked read-modify-write keyed on provider, sessionId and round with no task or thread component. All three defects are gone in this snapshot. ensure_unique_session_dir at lines 1355-1366 now calls candidate.mkdir() and only advances a counter when the OS itself raises FileExistsError, which is the correct atomic-allocation pattern rather than a check-then-create. locked_file at lines 73-113 takes a real cross-process byte lock through msvcrt.locking on Windows and fcntl.flock elsewhere, on a durable lock file, with a bounded 30-second acquisition deadline and unconditional release in a finally block. write_json_atomic at lines 116-129 writes to a temp name qualified by pid, thread id and 8 random bytes, opens it with the exclusive 'xb' mode, fsyncs before closing, then os.replace()s, and unlinks the temp file in a finally block. The evidence merge at lines 2360-2384 now runs the whole read, filter, append, sort and write inside locked_file, and the dedupe key is (provider, taskId, codexThreadId, sessionId, round). save_response at lines 2398-2403 raises rather than overwriting an already-saved response with different bytes. This is the mechanism AC7 needs and it is verified rather than attested.

findings.detail: The batch capacity acceptance entry lists six facts. Five are statements of enforced behaviour. Exactly one is an observation with a number in it: four fake children completed with maximum observed concurrency 3. There is no corresponding observed-maximum-6 datum anywhere in the evidence file. The asymmetry matters because the per-thread limit and the global limit are different code paths: a per-thread counter can be correct while a global counter double-counts, races on the capacity mutex boundary, or is evaluated before the mutex is taken. Given that the global cap is the one protecting the user's actual ChatGPT account from over-parallel use, it deserves the same style of evidence the per-thread cap already got. This is a gap in the evidence record rather than a demonstrated defect, and M3's two-task live run will exercise it anyway, but it should be closed with a recorded number rather than carried forward as an assertion.

pmReview.productManagerStatement: I recommend accepting this milestone. Two things were promised here. The first was to fix the unsafe file-writing inside the shared bridge that I warned you about last time, and I can confirm that one myself because those files are visible to me. Previously, when two requests finished at the same time, the code picked a folder name by checking whether it already existed and then creating it, which is a race two processes can lose together, and it rewrote the shared results file without any lock, so one result could silently erase another. Both are now done properly: folders are created in a single atomic step that the operating system itself guarantees, the shared results file is only ever touched while holding a genuine cross-process lock, and it is written to a temporary file, flushed to disk, and swapped into place in one move so a crash mid-write cannot leave you with a corrupted file. The record of which result belongs where now includes the task and the thread, not just the session, which was the specific way results could previously be confused between tasks. I also opened the tests behind the two headline numbers rather than taking them on trust: there really is a test that starts twenty sessions at once with deliberately identical names and demands twenty distinct folders, and one that runs ten simultaneous result-imports and demands all ten survive with the correct task and thread stamped on each. Those are real tests against the real code, and that is the strongest evidence in this milestone. The second promise was the scheduler that stops you ever running more than three requests for one task or six in total. That code lives in files the review snapshot deliberately does not show me, so my confidence there comes from the fingerprint matching, from 231 passing tests, and from one outside reviewer who read the changes and found nothing blocking. I want to be straight with you about four things, none of which justifies holding this up. First, the limit of six is stated as enforced but never actually measured. The only measurement recorded is four requests reaching a peak of three at once, which tests the per-task limit. The per-task and the global limits are different pieces of code, and the global one is the one protecting your ChatGPT account, so it deserves the same kind of measured proof and does not have it yet. Second, only one of your two outside reviewers ran again. Grok failed twice for the same setup fault as last time. The team did what I asked and wrote that fact plainly into the plan rather than hiding it, so this is now an accepted, visible choice rather than an oversight, but it means the most safety-critical code in this milestone had exactly one independent reader. Third, the new batch command is already described in the user-facing documentation but does not appear anywhere in the permanent tooling contract, which still describes only the older single-request command and still talks about this milestone's limits as future work. That update is already scheduled as the first step of the final milestone, and I would do it before the live test rather than after, so the real run is checked against a document that actually describes what is being run. Fourth, one test failed once under heavy load and was closed by re-running it successfully. That was a reasonable call, but on a milestone entirely about doing things at the same time, a passing re-run is the weakest possible evidence, so if anything similar happens during the live run it should be investigated rather than re-run. On the positive side, everything I asked for at the last gate was actually done: the two-hour default and the three special result names are now in the permanent contract with matching test obligations, your Chrome session booking moved to the start of the next stage, and there is now a step requiring someone to look at the waiting-time measurements before deciding whether anything needs to be fairer between competing tasks. Nothing was widened, no shortcut was added that would let a crashed request be resent, and nothing from the final milestone was pulled forward to make this one look bigger. Finally, be clear what you are accepting. About three quarters of the engineering is done, and not one of your eleven acceptance criteria is formally closed, because nothing has yet touched a real ChatGPT page. What remains is the part you can actually see and judge for yourself: three pages running at once for one task, two tasks running side by side without interfering, the fourth and seventh requests waiting quietly without opening anything, and a closed tab reopening at exactly its own address and nobody else's.

Acceptance of those three fixes rests on the recorded verdict, the now-named reviewed regions, the two durable-evidence negative facts and the spec text that encodes both rules.

risks.mitigation: Keep the labelled conclusion verbatim in the archived record, and capture the first real throttle observation as follow-up live evidence rather than upgrading the claim retroactively.
risks.statement: Site throttling behaviour, both the pre-send terminal failure and the post-click send-uncertain no-resend branch, is still proven only by M2 unit coverage. It is now explicitly labelled in two evidence files rather than implied by a ticked AC11, but it remains the one production condition certain to arrive unannounced on a live account.

risks.mitigation: Note in the archived evidence that the live queue proofs used a shortened timeout by design, and treat the first full-length production wait as an observation worth recording.
risks.statement: The 7200-second default was never exercised end to end; both queue proofs used roughly 30-second waits of 30039 and 30084 milliseconds. The default is held by spec text, the adapter pin and a literal unit assertion, and a two-hour wait is the setting under which a real user would first meet any long-timer defect.

risks.mitigation: Recompute the three source digests immediately before the Phase 3.4 commit, treat any movement from fcbef6b9/baf22992/2d24f607 as blocking, and re-stamp at the committed HEAD so the durable record and the commit agree.
risks.statement: The M3 attestation now binds the same HEAD as the workspace, but the workspace is dirty, so the recorded harnessTrackedDiffSha256 cannot be checked against the state under review and any adapter, watcher or bridge change between attestation and commit would sit outside every recorded check.

risks.mitigation: Rewrite the M3 completion-matrix row to completed/accepted with this review's evidence refs during the archive pass, so the durable record matches the user's acceptance at 14:33:18.962Z.
risks.statement: product-manager.json still carries an M3 completion-matrix row reading in_progress with pmVerdict null, userDecision rejected and empty evidenceRefs, plus requiredGatesPassed false, alongside a finalReview that records verdict accepted and userAccepted true. The archived record would show two contradictory states for the same milestone.

risks.mitigation: Treat the recorded 4-341 ms slot waits as the baseline; if a future report shows waits approaching the batch timeout, open a fairness requirement against that data rather than redesigning speculatively.
risks.statement: Cross-task fairness remains deliberately unbuilt while the caps that make starvation possible are enforced at the harness boundary. A starved task surfaces to a user as ConcurrencySlotTimeout, which is indistinguishable from a defect at the point of use.

risks.mitigation: Keep verify:sources and doctor in the standing pre-milestone gate set so any future unpublished pin fails early rather than at a final delivery review.
risks.statement: The authoritative CCG source is now published and fetchable, but the harness still asserts snapshot fidelity through a 13-file byte comparison plus verify:sources against a single pinned commit and tree. Nothing structurally prevents a future local-only pin from recreating the blockage that cost this milestone a review cycle.
